entry.title: Knowledge-Graph-Augmented RAG: How LightRAG Bridges Flat Retrieval and Structured Reasoning

link.title: Knowledge-Graph-Augmented RAG: How LightRAG Bridges Flat Retrieval and Structured Reasoning

entry.content:
Knowledge Graph RAG LightRAG Retrieval

Knowledge-Graph-Augmented RAG: How LightRAG Bridges Flat Retrieval and Structured Reasoning

Standard vector RAG retrieves text chunks by similarity — and hopes the LLM figures out the connections. LightRAG introduces a structured knowledge graph into the retrieval process, enabling multi-hop reasoning, entity-centric lookups, and dual-level retrieval that pure chunk similarity cannot achieve.

On this page
The Problem with Flat RAG What is LightRAG? Ingestion Pipeline KG Construction Query Modes Query Flow Example Storage Architecture LightRAG vs Standard RAG Caching & Performance Multimodal Support Practical Limitations When to Use LightRAG Sources

The Problem with Flat RAG

Standard vector RAG has a fundamental limitation: it represents documents as flat collections of chunks. Each chunk is embedded independently, and retrieval finds the top-K most similar chunks to the query. This works for simple factual questions but fails when:

Failure
Complex Inter-Dependencies
Information about how entities relate to each other is spread across multiple chunks. A flat search finds individual mentions but misses the relationships connecting them.
Failure
Multi-Hop Reasoning
Questions requiring traversal of relationships (A depends on B, B conflicts with C) cannot be answered by similarity search alone — the answer requires following a chain of connections.
Failure
Thematic Understanding
High-level questions about trends, patterns, or overarching themes require aggregating information across many documents — not just finding the most similar chunk.
The Core Issue

Flat data representation leads to fragmented answers and fails to capture complex inter-dependencies. The retrieval system has no understanding of structure — it only knows "this text is similar to that text."

What is LightRAG?

LightRAG is a retrieval-augmented generation framework that augments standard vector-based RAG with an automatically constructed knowledge graph. During ingestion, it extracts typed entities and binary relationships from your documents using an LLM, building a structured graph alongside the traditional vector index.

At query time, it performs dual-level retrieval — searching both the entity graph (for precise, local lookups) and the relationship graph (for thematic, global reasoning) — then merges results with relevant source chunks to provide comprehensive, context-rich answers.

Key Insight

LightRAG doesn't replace vector search — it augments it with graph structure. You get the semantic coverage of vector similarity PLUS the precision of explicit entity relationships. The graph tells you what's connected to what; the vectors tell you what's semantically relevant.

Ingestion Pipeline

The ingestion process transforms raw documents into a dual representation: a knowledge graph AND a vector index, both built from the same source material.

Document Processing Flow
Documents
PDF, text, HTML
→
Chunking
Token-based split
→
LLM Extraction
Entities + Relations
→
Graph Build
Merge + Deduplicate
→
Embed
Entities + Relations + Chunks
→
Store
Graph + Vector + KV
  • 1. Chunking
    Documents are split into token-sized chunks using a configurable tokenizer (default chunk size: ~1200 tokens, overlap: ~100 tokens).
  • 2. Entity & Relationship Extraction
    Each chunk is sent to an LLM with a structured prompt instructing it to extract typed entities (name, type, description) and binary relationships (source, target, keywords, description). Supports "gleaning" — multiple extraction passes on the same chunk to catch missed entities.
  • 3. Two-Phase Merge
    Extracted nodes and edges are merged into the knowledge graph — entities first, then relationships. Duplicate entities are merged; descriptions are aggregated or LLM-summarized. Source chunk IDs are tracked for provenance.
  • 4. Embedding
    Each entity, each relationship, and each source chunk gets its own vector embedding — stored in the vector database. This enables semantic search at three granularities: entity-level, relationship-level, and chunk-level.

Knowledge Graph Construction

The LLM-driven extraction produces a typed graph where:

Nodes
Typed Entities
Each entity has a name, type (person, organization, concept, technology, etc.), and a merged description aggregated from all chunks that mention it. Duplicates are detected and merged automatically.
Edges
Binary Relationships
Each relationship connects a source entity to a target entity, with keywords (for retrieval), a description (for context), and source chunk IDs (for provenance). Relationships are also embedded for semantic search.
Provenance
Source Tracking
Every entity and relationship tracks which source chunks it was extracted from. At query time, the system can retrieve the original text that supports any graph-derived answer — ensuring citations are always available.
Gleaning: Multi-Pass Extraction

A single LLM pass may miss entities or relationships — especially in dense technical text. LightRAG supports "gleaning": running the extraction prompt multiple times on the same chunk and merging results. This catches entities that one pass overlooked, improving graph completeness without additional source documents.

Query Modes: Local, Global, Hybrid, and Naive

LightRAG's dual-level retrieval system separates queries into two keyword types and routes them through different search paths:

Mode
Local Mode
Embeds low-level keywords (specific entities, names, terms) and queries the entities vector DB. Then traverses the graph from matched entities to collect connected relationships. Best for: precise entity-centric questions.
Mode
Global Mode
Embeds high-level keywords (themes, concepts, patterns) and queries the relationships vector DB. Then collects associated entities. Best for: thematic questions, trend analysis, overview queries.
Mode
Hybrid Mode
Runs both local and global paths plus optionally a direct chunk vector search. Merges results from all paths. Best for: complex questions that need both entity precision and thematic context.
Mode
Naive Mode
Standard vector similarity search over chunks only — no graph traversal. Serves as a baseline comparison and fallback when graph data is unavailable. Equivalent to traditional RAG.
Keyword Decomposition

Before retrieval, the LLM decomposes the user query into two keyword types: high-level (overarching themes like "economic growth", "security architecture") and low-level (specific entities like "Microsoft", "TLS 1.3"). This decomposition drives which retrieval path activates — local searches entity embeddings, global searches relationship embeddings.

Query Flow: End-to-End Example

Here's how a query traverses the system in hybrid mode:

  • 1. Keyword Extraction
    LLM decomposes "How did Company X expand its cloud services?" into low-level keywords ["Company X", "cloud services"] and high-level keywords ["expansion", "growth", "acquisition"].
  • 2. Vector Searches (Parallel)
    Entities VDB → matches ["Company X", "Azure", "GitHub"]. Relationships VDB → matches ["Company X→Azure", "Company X→GitHub"].
  • 3. Graph Traversal
    From "Company X" → finds edges to "Azure", "GitHub", "Office365". From "Company X→Azure" → finds related entities "DataCenters", "AI Services". Multi-hop paths reveal connections not visible in flat search.
  • 4. Chunk Collection
    Source chunk IDs from all matched entities and relationships are gathered. Chunks are scored by weight or vector similarity, deduplicated, and truncated to fit the token budget.
  • 5. Context Assembly
    Entities, relationships, and source chunks are formatted into a structured context string — providing the LLM with both graph-derived structure and supporting text evidence.
  • 6. LLM Generation
    The assembled context is passed to the LLM for final answer generation. The answer benefits from semantic relevance (vector), structural context (graph), and complete source text (chunks).

Storage Architecture: Four Layers

LightRAG uses a pluggable multi-backend storage architecture with four distinct layers:

LayerPurposeBackend Options
Graph StorageEntities, relationships, and their connectionsNetworkX (default), Neo4j, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, OpenSearch
Vector StorageEmbeddings for entities, relationships, and chunksNanoVectorDB (default), FAISS, Milvus, Qdrant, PostgreSQL (pgvector), OpenSearch
Key-Value StorageChunk text, entity descriptions, metadataJSON files (default), Redis, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, OpenSearch
Document StatusTracking which documents have been ingestedJSON files (default), PostgreSQL, MongoDB, OpenSearch
Unified Backend Option

For production deployments, backends like OpenSearch or PostgreSQL can serve as a unified storage layer — handling graph, vector, KV, and document status in a single managed service. This simplifies operations while maintaining the logical separation of concerns.

LightRAG vs Standard Vector RAG

DimensionStandard Vector RAGLightRAG
Data RepresentationFlat chunks with embeddingsChunks + Knowledge Graph (entities + relationships)
Retrieval MethodSimilarity search onlyDual-level: entity search + relationship search + graph traversal
Multi-Hop Reasoning✗ Cannot follow connections✓ Graph traversal across entity edges
Thematic Questions✗ Returns fragments✓ Global mode searches relationship embeddings
Entity-Centric LookupApproximate (similarity)✓ Explicit entity nodes with typed metadata
Ingestion CostEmbedding onlyEmbedding + LLM extraction (higher)
Query LatencyFast (single vector search)Moderate (vector + graph + merge)
ProvenanceChunk-level only✓ Entity→chunk, relationship→chunk tracing
Incremental Updates✓ Append new chunks✓ Merge new entities/relationships into existing graph

Caching & Performance

LightRAG implements multi-level caching to optimize both ingestion and query performance:

Ingestion
Document Status Cache
Tracks which documents have already been processed. Re-ingestion skips previously processed documents — only new or modified content triggers extraction. Enables efficient incremental updates.
Query
LLM Response Cache
Caches LLM responses for keyword extraction and answer generation. Identical queries return cached results without re-invoking the LLM — significantly reducing latency and cost for repeated questions.
Graph
Entity Merge Cache
During ingestion, entity deduplication and merge results are cached. When the same entity is encountered in new documents, the system merges descriptions without reprocessing the entire graph.

Multimodal Support

LightRAG extends beyond text through integration with multimodal processing pipelines (e.g., RAG-Anything). This enables knowledge graph construction from:

Source
Images & Diagrams
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) extract descriptions from images, architecture diagrams, and flowcharts — converting visual information into text that feeds the entity extraction pipeline.
Source
Tables & Structured Data
Tabular data is parsed and converted into entity-relationship triples. Column headers become entity types; rows become instances. Relationships between table entities are inferred and added to the graph.

Practical Limitations & Tradeoffs

LightRAG is powerful but not without cost. From hands-on experience, here are the real tradeoffs teams should plan for:

Cost
Graph Construction is Expensive
Entity and relationship extraction requires an LLM call for every chunk — often with multiple "gleaning" passes. For large document sets, initial graph construction can take hours and consume significant LLM tokens. However, incremental updates are supported — new documents get processed without rebuilding the entire graph.
Tuning
Parameter Sensitivity
The number of entities, relationships, and chunks to retrieve must be carefully tuned per use case. Too many results overload the LLM context window with irrelevant information, degrading answer quality. Too few miss critical context. Finding the right balance requires experimentation with your specific data and query patterns.
Latency
Slower Answer Generation
Compared to standard vector RAG, LightRAG adds latency: keyword extraction (LLM call), dual vector searches, graph traversal, chunk collection, and context assembly — all before the final generation call. Total query time is noticeably higher than a simple similarity search + generate pattern.
Quality
Extraction Quality Depends on the LLM
The knowledge graph is only as good as the LLM's extraction capability. Weaker models miss entities, invent relationships, or produce inconsistent typing. Using a capable model for extraction (even if you use a smaller model for query-time generation) is critical for graph quality.
Scale
Graph Growth Management
As the graph grows, entity merging becomes complex — duplicate detection across thousands of entities requires LLM-based summarization, adding cost. Graph traversal time also increases with edge count. Production deployments need a strategy for graph pruning or partitioning.
Debugging
Harder to Debug Than Standard RAG
When answers are wrong, the failure could be in extraction (bad entities), graph structure (missing edges), vector search (wrong matches), chunk selection (wrong source text), or generation. Multiple retrieval paths make root-cause analysis more complex than single-path vector RAG.

Strengths vs Limitations Summary

StrengthsLimitations
Multi-hop reasoning via graph traversalHigh initial ingestion cost (LLM calls per chunk)
Dual-level retrieval (entity + thematic)Higher query latency than standard vector RAG
Incremental updates without full rebuildParameter tuning required (entities/relations/chunk counts)
Provenance tracking (entity → source chunk)Extraction quality dependent on LLM capability
Handles thematic/overview questions wellGraph growth management at scale
Pluggable storage backendsMore complex debugging (multiple retrieval paths)
Automatic entity deduplication and mergeContext window overload risk if retrieval params not tuned
Open-source with active developmentEvaluation integration still maturing
The Incremental Update Advantage

Despite the high initial cost, LightRAG's incremental update capability is a significant operational benefit. When new documents arrive, only those documents are processed — new entities merge into the existing graph, new relationships extend it. You don't restart from scratch. This makes the upfront investment amortizable over time.

When to Use LightRAG

Good Fit
Documents with Rich Entity Relationships
Technical documentation, specifications, research papers — anywhere entities reference, depend on, or conflict with each other across documents.
Good Fit
Multi-Hop Questions
"What depends on X?" "If Y changes, what's affected?" — questions requiring traversal of relationships that standard search cannot answer.
Good Fit
Thematic Exploration
"What are the main trends in X?" "How does Y relate to Z at a high level?" — questions needing aggregation across many documents.
Less Ideal
Simple Factual Lookup
If your questions are always simple and self-contained within a single chunk, the overhead of graph construction may not justify the benefit. Standard vector RAG suffices.
The Takeaway

LightRAG shines when your documents contain interconnected knowledge — where understanding the relationships between entities is as important as finding the entities themselves. It's the middle ground between simple vector RAG (fast, flat) and full enterprise knowledge graphs (complex, manual) — automated graph construction with retrieval that leverages structure.

Sources & References

  • LightRAG GitHub Repository — Official implementation, source code, and documentation
  • LightRAG Research Paper — Architecture design, dual-level retrieval, and evaluation results
  • RAG-Anything — Multimodal extension for knowledge graph construction from images, diagrams, and tables
entry.summary: How LightRAG augments standard vector RAG with an automatically constructed knowledge graph — enabling multi-hop reasoning, entity-centric lookups, and dual-level retrieval that pure chunk similarity cannot achieve.

entry.title: From Words to Systems: The Evolution of the Agentic Stack

link.title: From Words to Systems: The Evolution of the Agentic Stack

entry.content:
Agentic AI Harness Engineering Loop Engineering Architecture

From Words to Systems: The Evolution of the Agentic Stack

The most important code in an agent system is not the agent itself — it is the code that wraps, constrains, and directs it. Over four years, the unit of engineering has shifted from a single prompt, to a context window, to a runtime harness, to an autonomous loop. Each layer didn't replace the previous; it absorbed it.

On this page
The Thesis The Four Layers Evolution Timeline Prompt Engineering Context Engineering Harness Engineering Loop Engineering Comparative Matrix Cross-Cutting Model Practical Implications What Comes Next

The Thesis: Words Cannot Constrain Compute

"You shouldn't be prompting coding agents anymore. You should be designing loops that prompt your agents."
— Peter Steinberger, June 2026

LLMs are probabilistic reasoning engines. Production systems demand deterministic behavior. This fundamental mismatch is what every layer of the agentic stack attempts to resolve.

Prompt engineering assumed you could phrase your way to reliability. You cannot. Context engineering recognized the problem wasn't wording — it was what the model could see. Harness engineering recognized the problem wasn't visibility — it was what the model could touch. Loop engineering recognized the problem wasn't a single action — it was the entire cycle of acting, evaluating, and continuing.

Each Layer is a Different Unit of Control

A prompt controls one model response. Context controls one invocation's information environment. A harness controls one agent's execution boundary. A loop controls one agent's behavior cycle over time. Each layer preserves the layer beneath it — a prompt doesn't disappear once a loop is built around it.

The Four Layers: Definition and Emergence

Layer 1 · 2022–2023
Prompt Engineering
Writing and structuring the instruction for a single model call. The only lever was language. Solved: getting a model to produce a useful single response. Failed: "linguistic optimism" — the assumption that clear phrasing guarantees compliance in multi-step autonomy.
Layer 2 · 2024–2025
Context Engineering
Designing exactly what the agent sees — not just the prompt, but the entire token configuration. RAG pipelines, file attachments, context compaction, prompt caching. Solved: keeping agents oriented across step 30. Failed: context rot — accumulated outputs degrade reasoning over long sessions.
Layer 3 · 2025–2026
Harness Engineering
The deterministic wrapper around a probabilistic model — tools, permissions, sandboxes, memory, validation gates. The agent physically cannot execute outside its boundary. Solved: making agents reliable for hours. Left open: when to act, when to stop, who escalates.
Layer 4 · 2026–Present
Loop Engineering
Designing structural controls around an agentic loop: state machines, iteration limits, tool boundaries, verification gates, and human escalation paths. Moves from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop. The system prompts the agent, not the human.

Evolution Timeline: From Manual Prompting to Autonomous Loops

The initiation point has shifted from human to system over four years. Click any era to see details:

2022
Manual Prompting
2023
Templates
2024
Tool-Augmented
2025
Context-Managed
2025–26
Harnessed
2026
Event-Triggered
2026+
Autonomous
Era of Linguistic Optimism

Manual Prompting — User types, model responds

Human initiates every turn. The only lever is language. No memory, no tools, no context management. Each interaction is independent. Phrasing is everything.

Layer 1: Prompt Engineering (2022–2023)

What it is: Writing and structuring the instruction for a single model call. Separate system prompts into labeled sections — background, instructions, tool guidance, output format — delineated with XML tags or Markdown headers.

Why it emerged: Early LLMs (GPT-3, ChatGPT) were single-turn. The only lever was language.

What it solved: Getting a model to produce a useful single response.

The Wall It Hit: Linguistic Optimism

The assumption that the model will behave if you phrase instructions clearly enough. In multi-hour autonomous execution, phrasing cannot prevent hallucination, unauthorized actions, or context drift. A prompt is a suggestion — it can be reasoned around, ignored, or misinterpreted.

Layer 2: Context Engineering (2024–2025)

What it is: Designing exactly what the agent sees — not just the prompt, but the entire token configuration in the context window. Includes RAG pipelines, file attachments, context restructuring into clean JSON payloads, and prompt caching to save up to 90% in token costs.

Why it emerged: As agents moved from single-turn to multi-step, the context window became a finite resource. The engineering problem shifted from "finding the right words" to "optimizing the utility of tokens against model constraints."

What it solved: Keeping the agent oriented across step 5, step 15, step 30.

The Wall It Hit: Context Rot

The gradual degradation of reasoning quality as context fills with accumulated tool outputs, prior responses, and stale instructions. Even with perfect context management, a finite window cannot hold infinite session history without loss.

Layer 3: Harness Engineering (2025–2026)

What it is: The discipline of designing the scaffolding — context delivery, tool interfaces, planning artifacts, verification loops, memory systems, and sandboxes — that surrounds an AI agent and determines whether it succeeds or fails on real tasks.

"Agent = Model + Harness. A harness is the deterministic wrapper around a probabilistic model. It reduces the space in which the model can be wrong."
— The core equation of harness engineering

Why it emerged: Production agents needed to run for hours, touch real systems, and make irreversible decisions. The model couldn't self-regulate.

The Seven Layers of a Production Harness

  • Normalization
    Standardize inputs before they reach the model.
  • Context Orchestration
    Manage what enters the context window and when.
  • Constraint Layer
    Define what the agent can and cannot do — permissions, tool access, action boundaries.
  • Gated Execution
    Require approval or verification before irreversible actions.
  • Validation & Repair
    Check outputs against expectations; auto-correct when possible.
  • Graceful Degradation
    Fall back safely when the model fails or tools are unavailable.
  • State Management
    Persist agent state across sessions, crashes, and resumptions.

The Five Structural Primitives

Primitive
Filesystem
Durable state + collaboration surface. If it's not in the repo, it doesn't exist for the agent.
Primitive
Code Execution
Autonomous problem-solving capability. The agent can run code to verify its own outputs.
Primitive
Sandbox
Isolation + verification. Actions execute in a contained environment before affecting production.
Primitive
Memory
Cross-session persistence. The agent remembers decisions, preferences, and context across invocations.
Primitive
Context Management
Compaction against context rot. Active management of what stays, what gets summarized, what gets dropped.
Evidence of Convergence

LangChain improved Terminal Bench 2.0 from 52.8% to 66.5% through pure harness changes — no model change. OpenAI shipped ~1M lines of production code without manually written source in a five-month experiment. The enabler in both cases was environment design, not model capability.

Layer 4: Loop Engineering (2026–Present)

"My job is to write loops."
— Boris Cherny, Head of Claude Code, Anthropic

What it is: The software engineering discipline of designing structural controls around an agentic loop: state machines, iteration limits, tool boundaries, verification gates, and human escalation paths. It makes loops that are not only capable but also safe, auditable, and deterministic enough for production.

The Three Functional Stages of a Loop

  • Observation
    The agent perceives its environment and current state.
  • Decision
    The agent reasons about what to do next.
  • Action & Evaluation
    The agent acts, then a separate process evaluates the result against a completion condition. The loop continues or terminates based on that evaluation.

The Maker/Checker Pattern

Separation of Concerns

The agent that writes code should never be the one grading it. A separate, independent process verifies the output. This separation is what makes asynchronous execution trustworthy — you're not relying on the same probabilistic system that produced the work to also judge it.

The Six Core Pillars

Pillar
Automations
Event-driven triggers — webhooks, timers, CI events, issue creation. The loop activates without human initiation.
Pillar
Worktrees
Isolated execution environments. Each loop iteration operates on a clean copy, preventing state pollution between runs.
Pillar
Skills
Reusable capability modules. Encapsulated procedures the loop can invoke without re-specifying instructions.
Pillar
MCP Connectors
External tool interfaces via Model Context Protocol. Standardized access to external services and data sources.
Pillar
Sub-Agents
Delegated parallel workers. Complex tasks fan out to specialized agents that report back to the orchestrating loop.
Pillar
External Memory
Persistent context across loop iterations — AGENTS.md, memory files, session state. The loop doesn't start from scratch.

Comparative Matrix: The Four Layers Side by Side

LayerObjectiveControl PointEnablesFailure Mode
PromptElicit a useful single responseThe instruction textSingle-turn Q&A, classification, generationLinguistic optimism — fails under multi-step autonomy
ContextOptimize what the agent seesThe token budget — RAG, caching, compactionMulti-step agents that survive step 30Context rot — accumulated outputs degrade reasoning
HarnessBuild the deterministic runtime boundaryTools, permissions, sandboxes, validation gatesProduction agents touching real systems for hoursMakes one agent reliable but doesn't define when/how to act
LoopDesign the autonomous behavior cycleCadence, triggers, delegation, verification, escalationFully autonomous systems on timers, events, CIOrchestration complexity; safety when no human is in the loop

The Cross-Cutting Mental Model

Many engineers treat context, harness, and loop as a sequential pipeline — data flows A → B → C. This is wrong. The correct model is cross-cutting: the harness and the loop are orthogonal axes that operate simultaneously.

Execution Architecture
Event / Timer / Human Request
What triggers the loop
Loop Controller
trigger → observe → decide → act → verify → continue/stop
Harnessed Runtime
tools, permissions, sandbox, memory, state, validation, observability
Model + Prompt + Context
The probabilistic reasoning engine
Harness Axis
Constrains WHAT — the runtime boundary. What the agent can see, touch, execute, persist, and recover from.
Loop Axis
Governs WHEN — the temporal control. When the agent runs, how it iterates, verifies, retries, escalates, and stops.
The Operating System Analogy

The prompt is a single syscall. The context is the process's memory space. The harness is the kernel's permission system — what the process can touch. The loop is the scheduler — when the process runs, for how long, and when it gets preempted. These aren't stages in a pipeline. They're orthogonal, always-on systems.

Practical Implications for Teams

Practice
Evaluate the Model-Harness Pair
A strong model performs poorly without stable interfaces, structured memory, and scoped permissions. A more modest model can outperform it when the harness reduces ambiguity and constrains destructive actions. Evaluate the system, not the model alone.
Practice
Document the Harness as First-Class
Make state-changing actions interruptible, resumable, and reversible. Apply least-privilege tool governance with explicit approval gates. The harness configuration is as important as the model selection.
Practice
Repository = Primary Interface
If something is not in the repo, it does not exist for the agent. Repository legibility — how easily an agent can find, read, and act on project knowledge — determines the capability ceiling.
Practice
Start Restrictive, Expand on Evidence
New agents begin with read-only permissions and mandatory checkpoints. Track violation rate. Expand permissions where violations would have been safe. Calibrate based on data, not assumptions.
The Co-Evolution Warning

Models trained with specific harnesses can become overfitted to those designs. Harness architecture choices have lasting consequences beyond the immediate task. Design for portability.

What Comes Next: Graph Engineering

The stack may not end at loops. A potential fifth layer — graph engineering — controls the organization of many agents rather than one agent's behavior cycle. Each layer preserves the layer beneath it, and the pattern suggests the next unit of control is multi-agent topology.

The Closing Thought

The evolution from prompt engineering to loop engineering is not a story of replacement. It's a story of containment. Each layer emerged because the previous one could not contain the complexity of real-world execution. The prompt contains the instruction. The context contains the information. The harness contains the execution. The loop contains the behavior over time. And the question for the next era is: what contains the loops?
entry.summary: How the agentic stack evolved from prompt engineering to loop engineering — four layers of control that didn't replace each other but absorbed each other.

entry.title: Enterprise Identity & Access Flow: Authentication & Authorization with Microsoft Entra ID

link.title: Enterprise Identity & Access Flow: Authentication & Authorization with Microsoft Entra ID

entry.content:
Identity Authentication Authorization Entra ID + AWS

Enterprise Identity & Access Flow: Authentication & Authorization

How Microsoft Entra ID acts as a centralized identity provider for enterprise environments — issuing SAML assertions, OIDC tokens, and OAuth 2.0 access tokens to enable single sign-on, application authentication, delegated API access, and secure service-to-service communication.

On this page
Overview Protocols Explained Flow 1: AWS Console SSO Flow 2: Application Login Flow 3: Delegated API Access Flow 4: Service-to-Service Flow Comparison Key Concepts JWT Deep Dive Cloudflare Access Tokens The Big Picture Benefits Architecture Diagram

Overview: The Identity Triangle

Enterprise identity flows involve three parties:

Party 1
Users (Employees)
Human users who need access to AWS accounts, web applications, or APIs. They authenticate with passwords, MFA, and conditional access policies.
Party 2
Microsoft Entra ID (Identity Provider)
The centralized identity provider that authenticates users, manages groups/directories, enforces policies (MFA, conditional access), and issues tokens/assertions to relying parties.
Party 3
Relying Parties (Service Providers)
AWS IAM Identity Center, web/mobile applications, and APIs (Microsoft Graph, Salesforce, internal services) that trust Entra ID to verify identity and grant access.
End-to-End Flow
👤
User
Requests access
→
🔐
Entra ID
Authenticates (MFA)
→
🎫
Token Issued
SAML / OIDC / OAuth
→
✅
Relying Party
Validates & grants access

Protocols Explained

ProtocolFull NamePurposeToken Type
SAMLSecurity Assertion Markup LanguageXML-based assertions for SSO — proving who the user is to service providersSAML Assertion (XML)
OIDCOpenID ConnectAuthentication layer on top of OAuth 2.0 — uses ID Tokens (JWT) to identify usersID Token (JWT)
OAuth 2.0Open Authorization 2.0Delegated and client credentials flows — used for authorization to protect APIsAccess Token (JWT)
SCIMSystem for Cross-domain Identity ManagementUser & group provisioning — automated lifecycle management across systemsN/A (provisioning protocol)
Authentication vs Authorization

Authentication proves who the user is (identity verification). Authorization determines what the user or application is allowed to do (permission granting). SAML and OIDC handle authentication. OAuth 2.0 handles authorization. In practice, these often work together in a single flow.

Flow 1: AWS Console SSO (SAML)

Purpose: Authenticate a user and provide access to AWS accounts via single sign-on.

  • 1. User opens AWS Console
    SP-Initiated flow — user navigates to the AWS sign-in page.
  • 2. Redirect to Entra ID
    AWS redirects the user to Entra ID for authentication.
  • 3. Entra ID authenticates user
    User provides credentials. Entra ID enforces MFA and conditional access policies.
  • 4. SAML Assertion issued
    Entra ID sends back a SAML Assertion containing: user identity (e.g., alice@company.com), groups (e.g., CloudAdmins), attributes, and role mapping.
  • 5. AWS IAM Identity Center validates
    IAM Identity Center validates the assertion and assigns the user to the appropriate IAM role.
  • 6. User accesses AWS accounts
    User assumes IAM roles in target accounts (Dev / Prod / Security) based on group membership.
SAML Assertion Contains

User Identity (e.g., alice@company.com) · Groups (e.g., CloudAdmins) · Attributes for role mapping · Signature from Entra ID for validation

Flow 2: Application Login (OIDC)

Purpose: Identify the user (authentication) for a web or mobile application.

  • 1. User opens application
    User navigates to a web or mobile application hosted on AWS or elsewhere.
  • 2. Redirect to Entra ID (OIDC)
    Application redirects to Entra ID's authorization endpoint with an OIDC request.
  • 3. Entra ID authenticates user
    User authenticates with MFA and policies applied.
  • 4. ID Token returned (JWT)
    Entra ID returns an ID Token to the application containing: user identity (sub), name, email, groups/roles, and other claims.
  • 5. Application validates token
    Application verifies the JWT signature, issuer, audience, and expiration — then establishes a session for the user.
ID Token Contains

User Identity (sub) · Name, Email · Groups / Roles · Other Claims · Signature · Expiration

Flow 3: API Access (OAuth 2.0 — Delegated)

Purpose: Authorize an application to access APIs on behalf of the user.

  • 1. User authenticated in application
    User is already logged into the application (via OIDC flow above).
  • 2. Application requests access token
    Application requests an access token from Entra ID on behalf of the user, specifying the target API and required scopes.
  • 3. Entra ID returns Access Token (JWT)
    Entra ID validates the request and returns an access token with scoped permissions (e.g., Mail.Read).
  • 4. Application calls API with token
    Application includes the access token in API requests (Authorization: Bearer header).
  • 5. API validates token and checks permissions
    The resource server (e.g., Microsoft Graph) validates the token signature, checks scopes and roles, and returns the requested data.
Access Token Contains

Scopes / Permissions (e.g., Mail.Read) · Audience (API) · User or App ID · Expiration · Issuer signature

Flow 4: Service-to-Service (OAuth 2.0 — Client Credentials)

Purpose: Authorize a service or application to access APIs without a user — machine-to-machine communication.

  • 1. AWS Service requests token
    A Lambda function, ECS task, or background service requests a token using Client Credentials (client ID + secret or certificate). No user is involved.
  • 2. Entra ID returns Access Token
    Entra ID authenticates the application (not a user) and returns an access token with app-level permissions.
  • 3. Service calls API with token
    The service uses the access token to call internal or external APIs.
  • 4. API validates token and checks app permissions
    The resource server validates the token and checks application roles/permissions (not user scopes).
Client Credentials Access Token Contains

App (client) Identity (e.g., employee-sync-service) · Roles / Permissions (e.g., HR.Read) · Audience (API) · Expiration · No user identity — this is purely application authorization

Flow Comparison

FlowProtocolWho InitiatesToken IssuedPurpose
AWS Console SSOSAML 2.0User (SP-initiated)SAML AssertionAuthenticate user, assign IAM roles
Application LoginOIDCUser (via app redirect)ID Token (JWT)Identify the user for the application
Delegated API AccessOAuth 2.0Application (on behalf of user)Access Token (JWT)Authorize API access with user's permissions
Service-to-ServiceOAuth 2.0 (Client Credentials)Service (no user)Access Token (JWT)Authorize machine-to-machine API access

Key Concepts

Concept
Authentication
Proves who the user is. Handled by SAML assertions and OIDC ID tokens. The identity provider (Entra ID) verifies credentials and issues proof of identity.
Concept
Authorization
Determines what the user or application is allowed to do. Handled by OAuth 2.0 access tokens with scopes and roles. The resource server enforces permissions.
Concept
Token
A digital credential (JWT) issued by Entra ID. Contains claims about the user or application — identity, permissions, audience, expiration. Cryptographically signed for tamper detection.
Concept
Assertion
A SAML statement issued by Entra ID — an XML document containing identity claims, group memberships, and attributes. Used specifically for SSO with legacy and enterprise service providers.
Concept
Role / Scope
A permission to perform an action on a resource. Scopes are delegated (user-consented, e.g., Mail.Read). Roles are application-level (admin-assigned, e.g., HR.ReadWrite.All).
Concept
Conditional Access
Policies in Entra ID that enforce conditions before granting access — require MFA, block risky sign-ins, restrict by location/device, or require compliant devices.

JWT: The Token Format That Powers Everything

JSON Web Token (JWT) is the standard format for OIDC ID Tokens and OAuth 2.0 Access Tokens. Understanding JWT is essential because it's the actual credential that moves between systems.

JWT Structure: Three Parts

eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjM0NTY3ODkwIn0.SflKxwRJSMeKKF2QT4fwpM...
Part 1
Header
Specifies the token type (JWT) and signing algorithm (RS256, ES256). Tells the relying party how to verify the signature.
Part 2
Payload (Claims)
The actual data — who the user is (sub), what they can do (scope/roles), who issued it (iss), who it's for (aud), and when it expires (exp). This is the identity/authorization information.
Part 3
Signature
Cryptographic signature created with the issuer's private key. The relying party verifies it using the issuer's public key — proving the token hasn't been tampered with and was issued by a trusted authority.

Where JWT Plays a Role

FlowJWT Token TypeWhat It ContainsWho Validates It
Application Login (OIDC)ID TokenUser identity, name, email, groupsThe application
Delegated API AccessAccess TokenScopes (e.g., Mail.Read), audience, user IDThe API / resource server
Service-to-ServiceAccess TokenApp identity, roles, audience (no user)The API / resource server
AWS Console SSONot JWT — uses SAML Assertion (XML)User identity, groups, attributesAWS IAM Identity Center
Why JWT Matters

JWTs are self-contained — the relying party can validate them without calling back to the identity provider. This makes them fast (no network round-trip for validation), scalable (no session state on the server), and portable (any service with the public key can verify them). The tradeoff: they can't be revoked until they expire.

Cloudflare Access Tokens: Zero Trust at the Edge

Cloudflare Access adds another layer to the identity flow — acting as a reverse proxy that enforces authentication at the network edge before traffic ever reaches your application.

How It Works

  • 1. User requests application URL
    Request hits Cloudflare's edge network first — before reaching the origin server.
  • 2. Cloudflare redirects to identity provider
    If no valid session exists, Cloudflare redirects the user to the configured IdP (Entra ID, Okta, Google, etc.) for authentication.
  • 3. IdP authenticates and returns token
    Entra ID (or other IdP) authenticates the user and returns a token to Cloudflare.
  • 4. Cloudflare issues CF Access JWT
    Cloudflare validates the IdP token and issues its own signed JWT (the "CF Authorization" token) as a cookie. This token contains the user's identity and policy decision.
  • 5. Request forwarded to application
    Cloudflare forwards the request to the origin with the CF Access JWT in a header (Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion). The application can validate this JWT to identify the user without implementing its own authentication.
Cloudflare Access JWT Contains

User email · Identity provider used · Audience (the Access application ID) · Issued-at and expiration times · Custom claims from access policies · Signed by Cloudflare's team-specific key (verifiable via /cdn-cgi/access/certs endpoint)

Where Cloudflare Fits in the Stack

Benefit
Zero Trust: Authenticate Before Reaching Origin
Applications don't need to be publicly exposed. Cloudflare blocks unauthenticated requests at the edge — the application only receives pre-authenticated traffic with a verified JWT.
Benefit
IdP-Agnostic Authentication Layer
Cloudflare Access works with any OIDC-compliant IdP (Entra ID, Okta, Google, GitHub, etc.). Applications validate one token format (CF JWT) regardless of which IdP authenticated the user.

The Big Picture: Everything Maps to a Question

The entire enterprise identity stack answers five fundamental questions:

QuestionAnswerMechanism
Who are you?AuthenticationEntra ID + SAML / OIDC
What are you allowed to do?AuthorizationOAuth 2.0 Access Tokens (scopes & roles)
Should an account exist?ProvisioningSCIM (automated user/group lifecycle)
How do you access AWS?AWS AccessSAML Federation → IAM Identity Center → IAM Roles
Is the request trustworthy?Zero Trust (edge)Cloudflare Access → JWT at the edge

Protocol-to-Purpose Mapping

SAML
AWS Access = SAML Federation
SAML Assertion → IAM Identity Center → IAM Roles. The user authenticates once and gets federated access to multiple AWS accounts based on group membership.
OIDC
Application Login = OIDC ID Tokens
The application learns who the user is via a signed JWT. No password stored in the application — identity is delegated to the trusted provider.
OAuth 2.0
API Access = OAuth Access Tokens
Applications call APIs with scoped access tokens — either on behalf of a user (delegated) or as a service (client credentials). Least-privilege by design.
SCIM
Provisioning = Automated Lifecycle
When a user joins or leaves the organization in Entra ID, SCIM automatically creates, updates, or deactivates their accounts in downstream applications — no manual provisioning.

Key Benefits

Benefit
Single Sign-On (SSO)
One authentication event grants access to all enterprise applications and AWS accounts. Users authenticate once with Entra ID and access everything without re-entering credentials.
Benefit
Centralized Security Policies
MFA, conditional access, and risk-based authentication are enforced at the identity provider level — not per-application. One policy change applies everywhere.
Benefit
Fine-Grained Authorization
OAuth scopes enable least-privilege access — applications request only the permissions they need. No over-provisioning of credentials.
Benefit
Secure Service-to-Service
Machine-to-machine communication uses short-lived tokens instead of stored user credentials. No passwords in config files. Tokens expire automatically.

Architecture Diagram

The complete enterprise identity and access flow — showing all four patterns (SAML SSO, OIDC login, delegated OAuth, and client credentials) with Microsoft Entra ID as the centralized identity provider:

Click to expand
entry.summary: A comprehensive guide to enterprise identity flows — how Microsoft Entra ID integrates with AWS and applications using SAML, OIDC, and OAuth 2.0 for single sign-on, delegated access, and service-to-service authorization.

entry.title: Beyond ‘It Looks Good’: A Production RAG Evaluation Framework

link.title: Beyond ‘It Looks Good’: A Production RAG Evaluation Framework

entry.content:
RAG Evaluation LLM-as-Judge RAGAS AWS Bedrock

Beyond "It Looks Good": A Production RAG Evaluation Framework

If you can't measure the quality of your RAG system, you can't confidently improve it. This guide covers how to build a production-grade evaluation framework — comparing open-source (RAGAS) with managed (Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations), with architecture patterns for offline, online, and CI/CD-integrated pipelines.

On this page
Why RAG Evaluation? Evaluation Lifecycle Evaluation as a Pipeline Metrics Taxonomy Quantitative vs Qualitative Architecture Patterns RAGAS Deep Dive AgentCore Evaluations Framework Comparison CI/CD Integration Custom Rubrics Maturity Model

Why RAG Evaluation Matters

Teams spend weeks experimenting with embedding models, chunking strategies, rerankers, prompts, and LLMs. A change may feel like an improvement because it produces a few impressive examples — but without structured evaluation, there is no objective way to answer:

Question
Did retrieval actually improve?
Changing the embedding model or chunk size might help some queries and hurt others. Without metrics, you'll never know the net effect.
Question
Did hallucinations decrease?
A model upgrade that sounds more fluent might actually hallucinate more. Faithfulness metrics catch this before users do.
Question
Is the newer model worth the cost?
A 3x more expensive LLM that only improves answer quality by 2% might not justify the spend. Evaluation quantifies the tradeoff.
The Real Problem

RAG systems have multiple moving parts — ingestion, chunking, embedding, retrieval, reranking, prompting, and generation. If the final answer is wrong, the problem could be at any stage. Without evaluating each stage independently, debugging becomes guesswork.

The Evaluation Lifecycle

Evaluation is not a one-time activity — it's a continuous cycle that begins before the system is even deployed. The lifecycle starts with synthetic test set generation and loops back through human review at every stage.

  • 1. Synthetic Test Set Generation
    LLMs automatically generate evaluation questions, expected answers, and relevant contexts from your enterprise documents. This creates a representative benchmark dataset without months of manual curation. Tools like RAGAS TestsetGenerator or custom prompting pipelines produce diverse question types — factual, multi-hop, reasoning, comparison — covering the breadth of real user queries.
  • 2. Human Review & Curation
    Domain experts review the synthetic test set — validating questions for relevance, correcting expected answers, removing duplicates, and adding edge cases that synthetic generation missed. This human-in-the-loop step transforms a rough synthetic set into a golden benchmark dataset that reflects real-world complexity.
  • 3. Run Evaluation Against the Agent
    Execute the curated test set against the RAG system. Collect traces (question → retrieved context → generated answer) and compute metrics across retrieval and generation stages. This establishes the performance baseline.
  • 4. Iterate on Configuration Changes
    Whenever the agent configuration changes — new embedding model, updated chunking strategy, prompt modification, LLM upgrade, reranker tuning — re-run the evaluation against the same golden dataset. This ensures every change is measured, not assumed to be an improvement.
  • 5. Compare Results Against Baseline
    Generate per-question verdicts (PASS / IMPROVE / FAIL) by comparing candidate scores against the baseline. Use weighted metric thresholds to determine whether the change is a net positive. Identify regressions early — before they reach production.
  • 6. Human Review of Results & Feedback Loop
    Stakeholders and domain experts review evaluation results — especially low-scoring questions and borderline verdicts. Their feedback feeds back into the cycle: updating the test set with new edge cases, refining expected answers, adjusting metric weights, or identifying areas where the rubric itself needs improvement.
Why Start with Synthetic Generation?

Creating evaluation datasets manually is expensive and slow — typically taking weeks for a team to produce a few hundred questions. Synthetic generation produces thousands of diverse questions in hours, covering corner cases humans wouldn't think to test. The human review step then ensures quality without the bottleneck of manual creation from scratch.

The Feedback Loop is Critical

Step 6 is what separates mature evaluation from a one-shot benchmark. Human feedback refines the test set over time — adding questions that exposed real production failures, removing outdated questions after system changes, and continuously raising the quality bar. The golden dataset evolves with the system.

Evaluation as a Pipeline

Rather than evaluating only the final answer, production systems evaluate multiple stages independently. This separation identifies exactly where quality is lost.

  • Stage 1: Retrieval Evaluation
    Did the system retrieve the right information? Measures whether relevant documents make it into the context window.
  • Stage 2: Generation Evaluation
    Did the LLM use the retrieved context correctly? Checks faithfulness, relevance, and completeness of the generated answer.
  • Stage 3: End-to-End Evaluation
    Does the overall system meet user expectations? Measures task success, latency, cost, safety, and user satisfaction.
Key Insight

A system can have perfect retrieval but poor generation (LLM ignores context), or perfect generation but poor retrieval (right answer for the wrong reasons). Evaluating stages independently reveals which component to optimize.

Metrics Taxonomy

Retrieval Metrics

MetricWhat It MeasuresWhy It Matters
Context PrecisionHow much retrieved context is relevantLess noise reaching the LLM = fewer hallucinations
Context RecallDid retrieval find all important informationMissing context = incomplete answers
Hit Rate (Hit@K)Was the correct doc in top K resultsBaseline retrieval effectiveness
MRRHow highly the correct doc appearsHigher rank = better LLM attention
NDCGRanking quality with graded relevanceRewards placing best docs at the top

Generation Metrics

MetricWhat It MeasuresWhy It Matters
FaithfulnessIs every claim supported by contextDirectly measures hallucination — the #1 stakeholder concern
Answer RelevanceDoes the answer address the questionCatches technically correct but off-topic responses
CompletenessDoes the answer cover all aspectsPartial answers frustrate users
CorrectnessHow close to a reference answerGround-truth comparison when available
Context UtilizationDid the model use the retrieved contextExcellent context retrieved but ignored = wasted retrieval

End-to-End Metrics

Task
Success Rate
Latency
Response Time
Cost
Per Query
Hallucination
Rate
Safety
Compliance

Quantitative vs Qualitative Evaluation

Statistical
Quantitative Metrics
Objective numerical scores: Precision, Recall, Hit Rate, MRR, NDCG, ROUGE, BLEU, METEOR. Repeatable, easy to compare over time, integrated into dashboards. But can't capture nuance.
LLM-as-Judge
Qualitative Metrics
An LLM evaluates outputs against criteria: helpfulness, faithfulness, clarity, groundedness, completeness. Scales better than human review while capturing nuances statistical metrics miss.

The most effective evaluation strategies combine both — statistical metrics for regression detection and automated benchmarking, LLM-as-Judge for quality dimensions that require reasoning.

Architecture: Offline, Online, and Hybrid

A production evaluation system operates across three modes:

Pre-Deploy
Offline (Batch) Evaluation
Run against curated benchmark datasets before deployment. Compare candidate vs baseline using golden datasets. Gate deployments on metric thresholds. Regression testing for every change.
Post-Deploy
Online (Live) Evaluation
Continuously monitor production traffic. Sample a percentage of sessions (e.g., 10%). Track quality trends over time. Alert on degradation. No golden dataset needed — evaluates against rubrics.
On-Demand
Targeted Investigation
Evaluate specific sessions or traces. Investigate reported issues. Validate fixes. Analyze historical data. Useful for debugging and root-cause analysis of quality problems.

Evaluation Pipeline Architecture

  • Ingest
    Collect agent traces (question, retrieved context, generated answer, tool calls) — via OpenTelemetry, application logs, or direct API capture.
  • Enqueue
    Queue evaluation jobs (SQS, Kafka, or managed service). Decouple evaluation from the serving path to avoid latency impact.
  • Evaluate
    Workers execute metric computations — statistical metrics in parallel with LLM-as-Judge scoring. Multiple evaluators run concurrently per trace.
  • Store
    Persist scores with full lineage (trace ID, evaluator version, model used). Enables historical trending and A/B comparison.
  • Verdict
    Compare against baselines — generate PASS/IMPROVE/FAIL verdicts per question using configurable thresholds and weighted metrics.
  • Report
    Dashboard visualization, CloudWatch metrics for alerting, natural-language summaries for stakeholders, and CI/CD gate decisions.

RAGAS: Open-Source Evaluation

RAGAS (Retrieval Augmented Generation Assessment) is the most widely adopted open-source framework for RAG evaluation. It provides both retrieval and generation metrics, all computed using LLM-as-Judge under the hood.

Core Metrics

MetricCategoryWhat It Evaluates
FaithfulnessGenerationClaims in the answer supported by retrieved context
Answer RelevancyGenerationWhether the answer addresses the question asked
Answer CorrectnessGenerationSemantic similarity to a reference answer
Answer SimilarityGenerationSurface-level similarity to reference
Context PrecisionRetrievalProportion of retrieved context that is relevant
Context RecallRetrievalProportion of relevant information retrieved
Context Entity RecallRetrievalNamed entities from ground truth found in context
Context UtilizationGenerationHow effectively the model uses retrieved context

Agentic Evaluation Metrics

For multi-turn agent interactions, RAGAS provides:

Agent
Agent Goal Accuracy
Did the agent achieve the user's stated goal across the full multi-turn interaction? Evaluates end-to-end task completion.
Agent
Tool Call Accuracy
Did the agent invoke the correct tools with the right parameters? Measures whether the agent's reasoning led to appropriate tool selection.
RAGAS Strengths

No vendor lock-in. Fully extensible. Works with any LLM provider. Integrates into CI/CD pipelines. Active open-source community. Supports custom metrics. Reference-free evaluation possible (no golden dataset required for some metrics).

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations

AgentCore Evaluations is AWS's managed evaluation service. It uses LLM-as-Judge techniques with both built-in and custom evaluators, integrating with OpenTelemetry and OpenInference instrumentation.

Evaluation Types

Continuous
Online Evaluation
Monitors live production traffic continuously. Configurable sampling (e.g., 10% of sessions). Conditional filters for targeted evaluation. Aggregated dashboards with trend tracking.
Targeted
On-Demand Evaluation
Evaluate specific spans or traces by ID. Investigate customer interactions. Validate fixes. Analyze historical data. Ideal for build-time testing and issue investigation.
Bulk
Batch Evaluation
Process multiple sessions in a single async job. Supports ground truth via session metadata. Pre/post comparison for prompt or model updates. Regression testing across curated sets.

Built-in Evaluators

AgentCore provides pre-configured evaluators accessible via ARN (e.g., Builtin.Helpfulness). These use optimized prompt templates and cannot be modified — ensuring consistent scoring baselines.

Custom Evaluators

Define domain-specific evaluation criteria with custom prompt templates and evaluator models. Custom evaluators are private resources with IAM-based access control — enabling team-specific quality criteria without exposing evaluation logic.

AgentCore Strengths

Fully managed — no infrastructure to maintain. Native integration with Strands and LangGraph agents. OpenTelemetry trace ingestion. Session sampling and filtering. Aggregate dashboards built-in. Supports up to 1M input/output tokens per minute per account.

Framework Comparison: RAGAS vs AgentCore Evaluations

DimensionRAGAS (Open Source)Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
DeploymentSelf-hosted (your infra)Fully managed (AWS)
LLM ProviderAny (OpenAI, Bedrock, local)Bedrock models
Retrieval Metrics✓ Context Precision, Recall, Entity Recall~ Via custom evaluators
Generation Metrics✓ Faithfulness, Relevancy, Correctness✓ Helpfulness, Correctness (built-in)
Agentic Metrics✓ Goal Accuracy, Tool Call Accuracy✓ Goal attainment, tool accuracy
NLP Metrics~ Via integration✗ Not built-in
Online Evaluation~ Build your own pipeline✓ Native with sampling + filters
Batch Evaluation✓ With custom orchestration✓ Managed async jobs
Custom Rubrics✓ Fully extensible✓ Custom evaluators with IAM
CI/CD Integration✓ Native (Python, any CI)✓ Via SDK/CLI
Ground Truth Support✓ Reference-based + reference-free✓ Via session metadata
Dashboards✗ Build your own✓ Built-in aggregation
Trace Integration~ Manual✓ OpenTelemetry native
Vendor Lock-in✓ None✗ AWS
CostLLM inference costs onlyLLM inference + service fees
Best ForTeams needing full control, multi-cloudTeams on AWS wanting managed ops

CI/CD Integration: Evaluate Before You Ship

Every change to a RAG system — embedding model, chunk size, retriever, reranker, prompt, LLM — should be validated against evaluation benchmarks before deployment.

CI/CD Evaluation Pipeline

  • Trigger
    PR or commit triggers evaluation workflow (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, or any CI).
  • Run Candidate
    Execute the changed RAG system against the golden evaluation dataset. Collect traces (question, context, answer).
  • Evaluate
    Run RAGAS metrics (or AgentCore batch evaluation) on collected traces. Compute all configured metrics.
  • Compare
    Compare candidate scores against the baseline. Generate per-question verdicts (PASS / IMPROVE / FAIL) with configurable thresholds.
  • Gate
    Block deployment if weighted metric score drops below threshold. Report results as PR comments or CI annotations.
  • Promote
    On pass, the candidate becomes the new baseline. Store results for historical tracking.
A/B Testing in Practice

Instead of relying on intuition, run A/B tests against the same evaluation dataset. Compare retrieval metrics, generation metrics, latency, and cost. Only promote changes that demonstrate measurable improvements across the metric set.

Custom Domain-Specific Rubrics

Generic metrics are rarely sufficient in enterprise environments. A technically correct answer may still fail because it omitted required information, violated policies, or missed domain-specific criteria.

Domain
Regulatory Compliance
Does the answer comply with industry regulations? Are required disclaimers present? Are citations to approved sources included?
Domain
Citation Completeness
Are all factual claims traced to a source? Are references valid and verifiable? Does the citation format match organizational standards?
Domain
Business Rule Validation
Does the answer respect business constraints? Are deprecated configurations flagged? Are prerequisite conditions mentioned?
Domain
Knowledge Coverage
Does the answer utilize all relevant internal knowledge? Are cross-references to related topics included? Is context from multiple sources synthesized?

Both RAGAS and AgentCore support custom rubrics — RAGAS through extensible Python classes, AgentCore through custom evaluator resources with configurable prompt templates.

Evaluation Maturity Model

Teams don't need to build everything at once. A practical path to production-grade evaluation:

  • Level 1: Manual Spot-Checks
    Human reviewers sample outputs periodically. No automation. High cost, low coverage. Where most teams start.
  • Level 2: Offline Benchmarks
    Golden dataset + automated RAGAS metrics in a notebook. Run before major changes. First measurable quality baseline.
  • Level 3: CI/CD-Gated Evaluation
    Every PR runs evaluation automatically. Deployment blocked on metric regression. Verdict system compares candidate vs baseline.
  • Level 4: Online Monitoring
    Live traffic evaluated continuously. Dashboards track trends. Alerts on quality degradation. Sampling-based to control cost.
  • Level 5: Continuous Optimization
    Evaluation drives automated A/B testing. System self-optimizes (prompt tuning, retrieval strategy selection) based on metric feedback loops.
The Bottom Line

The most successful teams treat evaluation as a first-class component of their architecture — just as important as retrieval, prompting, or model selection. A mature framework combines statistical metrics for objectivity, LLM-as-Judge for nuance, custom rubrics for domain relevance, and continuous monitoring for production safety.
entry.summary: A practical guide to building production-grade RAG evaluation — comparing RAGAS and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations, with architecture patterns for offline, online, and CI/CD-integrated evaluation pipelines.

entry.title: Knowledge Fabric: AI-Powered Technical Intelligence
entry.content:
Knowledge Graph RAG AI Agent Architecture

Knowledge Fabric: AI-Powered Technical Intelligence

A multi-layer architecture that transforms scattered technical documentation into an AI-queryable intelligence layer — connecting entities, parameters, dependencies, and metrics into a unified, traversable graph that an AI agent can reason over in a single round.

Architecture Pattern Multi-Layer Retrieval Entity-First Design Citation-Mandatory
On this page
The Problem What is a Knowledge Fabric? Architecture Query Traversal Why Not Standard RAG? Data Ingestion The AI Agent Access Patterns Design Principles Performance

The Problem: Documentation at Scale

Enterprise technical documentation is vast, distributed, and interconnected in ways no single search tool can navigate. Engineers face thousands of documents across dozens of formats — feature descriptions, configuration guides, parameter references, deployment procedures, impact reports, and performance metrics — each maintained by different teams, versioned independently, and cross-referencing each other implicitly.

The Real Cost

Traditional approaches — keyword search, manual cross-referencing, tribal knowledge — fail silently. Engineers get answers that are incomplete, outdated, or disconnected from the relationships that determine whether a configuration is safe to deploy.

Fragmented Information
Critical knowledge spans hundreds of documents. A single configuration decision may require cross-referencing feature descriptions, parameter guides, dependency trees, and deployment procedures.
Hidden Dependencies
Conflicts between features are buried in prose. Prerequisites are implicit. Impact chains traverse multiple document types. No single view connects them.
Version Drift
Documentation evolves across releases. Parameters change defaults, features get deprecated, new dependencies emerge. Keeping track manually doesn't scale.

What is a Knowledge Fabric?

A Knowledge Fabric is not a single database or a simple RAG pipeline. It is a multi-layer intelligence architecture where each layer specializes in a different type of retrieval — and an AI agent dynamically selects which layers to activate based on what the question requires.

The key insight: different questions need different retrieval strategies. A question about parameter values needs structured lookup. A question about dependencies needs graph traversal. A question about "how to deploy X" needs semantic search over procedural documentation. The Knowledge Fabric provides all of these through a unified interface.

Core Principle: Entity-First Resolution

Every query begins by resolving "what is this?" — determining the entity type (feature, parameter, metric, configuration class) before deciding "what about it?" This sub-100ms resolution step determines which layers are relevant, eliminating brute-force scanning across the entire corpus.

Architecture: Seven Interconnected Layers

The fabric is composed of specialized layers, each optimized for a different retrieval pattern. The layers are not isolated — they share entity identifiers, enabling cross-layer traversal in a single agent round.

1
Lexical
Entity Registry — name-to-type resolution. Acronym expansion. First hop for every query: determines routing to the correct downstream layer. Sub-100ms lookup.
2
Semantic
Vector embeddings with hybrid retrieval (kNN + BM25 + Reciprocal Rank Fusion). Entity-enriched metadata per chunk. Source-weighted boosting for high-value document types.
3
Relational
Knowledge graph of entities and their relationships — dependencies, conflicts, constraints, parameter sharing. Supports BFS traversal, topological sort, transitive impact analysis, and activation ordering.
4
Hierarchical
Parent-child containment trees for configuration objects. Maps which metrics belong to which configuration classes, with full attribute metadata (defaults, ranges, enumerations).
5
Structured
Typed fact tables — parameters, metrics, configuration steps, prerequisites, recommendations per deployment scenario. Precise point lookups with no ambiguity.
6
Temporal
Version evolution tracking — what was introduced, modified, or removed across releases. Enables release diff, deprecation tracking, and historical context for configuration decisions.
7
Bridge
Cross-domain index connecting entities across layers. Enables multi-hop queries: Feature → Configuration Class → Metrics, or Feature → Recommendation → Deployment Scenario.
Layer Interconnection

Every entity lives in multiple layers with shared identifiers. The Lexical layer resolves the entity and routes to the correct layer. The Bridge layer connects entities across domain boundaries. The Semantic layer fills gaps where structured data doesn't exist. No layer works in isolation.

How a Question Traverses the Fabric

When a user asks a question, the AI agent doesn't search all layers. It uses entity resolution to determine which layers are relevant, then executes tool calls in parallel — all in a single round. Click a question below to see which layers activate:

Select a query path:
Click a question to see the traversal path through the fabric layers.

Why Not Standard RAG?

Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation retrieves text chunks based on semantic similarity and passes them to an LLM. This works for simple questions but fails on the types of queries enterprise engineers actually ask:

Standard RAG
Retrieves text, hopes LLM figures it out
Finds documents mentioning an entity. Cannot traverse relationships, check constraints, compare versions, or resolve entity types. No structured precision — everything is fuzzy matching.
Knowledge Fabric
Understands structure, traverses relationships
Knows what an entity is, what depends on it, what conflicts with it, and what changed about it. Combines graph precision with semantic coverage. Every answer is cited.
The Difference in Practice

Standard RAG: "Find documents mentioning Feature X" → returns 20 loosely relevant chunks.
Knowledge Fabric: "What depends on Feature X, what conflicts with it, what parameters does it control, and what's the recommended configuration for Scenario Y?" → returns a structured, cited, traversal-backed answer in one round.

Data Ingestion: Keeping the Fabric Fresh

A Knowledge Fabric is only as good as its data currency. The ingestion pipeline transforms raw documents into the multi-layer representation automatically — no manual curation required.

  • Document Acquisition
    Automated detection and download of new or updated documents from source repositories. Multiple formats: PDF, HTML, JSON, XML, Excel.
  • Parsing & Extraction
    Domain-specific parsers extract structured content — tables, parameters, entities, relationships, metrics, and cross-references from each document type.
  • Entity Resolution & Registration
    Every extracted entity is resolved against the entity registry. New entities are registered with their type. Duplicates and aliases are merged.
  • Graph Construction
    Relationships between entities are materialized as graph edges — dependencies, conflicts, containment, parameter ownership, metric mapping.
  • Embedding & Indexing
    Text content is chunked, enriched with entity metadata, embedded, and indexed in the vector store with hybrid retrieval configuration.
  • Cross-Link Materialization
    Bridge layer indices are rebuilt — connecting entities across domain boundaries for multi-hop traversal.

The AI Agent: One Round, All Parallel

The Knowledge Fabric is accessed through a tool-equipped AI agent that orchestrates retrieval across layers. The agent's design follows a strict set of principles:

Routing
Entity-First Routing
Every query starts with entity resolution. The agent identifies what the user is asking about before deciding how to retrieve information. This prevents wasted tool calls and ensures precision.
Execution
Parallel Tool Execution
The agent calls all required tools in a single parallel block. It never chains sequential calls where parallel execution is possible. This minimizes latency and maximizes throughput.
Integrity
Citation-Mandatory Output
Every factual claim in the response must trace to a specific tool result. Claims without citations are treated as hallucinations and removed. The agent renders tool results — it never invents.
Priority
Structured Over Semantic
When structured data (typed facts, graph relationships) is available, it takes precedence over semantic retrieval. Semantic search fills gaps — it doesn't override precision.

Multiple Access Patterns

The Knowledge Fabric is consumed through multiple interfaces, each suited to different workflows:

IDE
MCP Protocol — IDE Integration
Model Context Protocol server exposes the fabric's tools directly inside coding assistants (Claude Code, Copilot). Engineers query documentation without leaving their development environment.
Visual
Interactive Dashboard
Visual exploration interface with chat, graph visualization, dependency viewers, timeline comparisons, and scenario planners. For deep investigation and planning workflows.
Programmatic
REST API
Programmatic access for CI/CD integration, automated validation, and batch queries. Enables fabric-powered checks in deployment pipelines.
Reasoning
Conversational Agent
Full reasoning agent for complex multi-step queries that require planning, traversal across multiple layers, and synthesized answers from diverse sources.

Design Principles

Principle
Entity-First Resolution
Every query resolves "what is this?" before "what about it?" The entity registry provides sub-100ms type resolution, enabling the system to skip irrelevant layers entirely and route to the correct retrieval path.
Principle
Graph + Semantic Fusion
Structured graph for precision (conflicts, dependencies, constraints). Semantic search for coverage (fuzzy matching, cross-document discovery, procedural knowledge). Neither alone is sufficient.
Principle
Zero Hallucination by Design
Every claim traces to a source. No citation = assertion deleted. The agent is instructed to render tool results, not synthesize from parametric memory. Structured data always overrides semantic guesses.
Principle
Always Fresh
Automated pipelines detect new documents, parse them, extract entities and relationships, update the graph, and re-index — keeping the fabric current without manual intervention.
